articles.description:
In January, I made a bet with myself:
No Copilot. No ChatGPT. No Claude. No AI-assisted anything for 30 days.
Not because I think AI is bad. I'm not that person.
But I noticed something creeping in — I was shipping code I couldn't fully explain. PRs went up faster, but when a colleague asked "why did you do it this way?" I'd pause. 🫠
The answer was always some version of:
"The AI suggested it. It worked."
That scared me more than any "AI will replace developers" headline ever could.
📋 Week 1:
I felt like I was coding with one hand tied behind my back.
Everything took longer. I Googled things I hadn't Googled in months. I read docs. Actual docs. MDN became my best friend again.
But here's the thing — I understood what I was writing. Every line had a reason I could articulate.
I wasn't fas…
articles.title: I Stopped Using AI Tools for 30 Days. Here's What I Learned About Myself as a Developer. 🚫🤖

articles.description:
Originally published on FreeDevKit.
Understanding Vector Embeddings in AI and Machine Learning Vector embeddings are numerical representations of real-world objects, such as words, phrases, images, or entire documents, transformed into a multi-dimensional space. These dense vectors capture the semantic meaning and contextual relationships of the original data, allowing machines to understand and process information in a way that mirrors human comprehension. By converting complex data into points in a high-dimensional vector space, algorithms can quantify the similarity or relatedness between different data points, which is fundamental to modern AI applications like semantic search, recommendation systems, and natural language processing (NLP).

Aligned with current Google and web standards
Built around free, privacy-first browser tools

articles.author: Prithvi Tomar
articles.description:
Your CRM knows when a customer goes quiet. It has no idea why that customer bought in the first place.


How it's wired



class HindsightWrapper:
    """Thin, opinionated wrapper over hindsight-client 0.5.0."""

    @property
    def raw(self) -> Hindsight:
        """Escape hatch to the underlying SDK client. Avoid unless needed."""
        return self._client

The single sentence in the per-customer bank's reflect mission that changed everything: "When asked about retention or churn, I always reference the conversion-phase memories that established this customer's decision profile." Without it, the agent grounds reasoning in whatever's most recent — which for a churn signal is always the silence. With it, the agent reaches back months automatically. I tweaked that string more carefully than I tweaked any actual Python code.

https://cross-live-intiligent.vercel.app/) with the following github repo (https://github.com/prithvi471/cross-live-intiligent)
Composed real data from Retailrocket, Amazon Reviews 2023, and Customer Support on Twitter, grounded in published retention research from Bain & Company, Forrester, and Frederick Reichheld at Harvard Business Review.
articles.title: # Same churn signal, two different right answers

articles.description:
I've been thinking about this for a while now and I'm not sure I have it fully figured out, but the more I work with AI agents on brownfield codebases the more I'm convinced that we've been protecting the wrong thing.
We treat code like it's the asset. We refactor it, we write tests for it, we argue about naming conventions and folder structure. And for a long time that made sense because rewriting was expensive, migration was risky, and the code was the only thing that actually knew how the system worked.
But that last part was always the problem, the code knows what it does but it doesn't know why. It doesn't know what was considered and rejected. It doesn't know that the bcrypt requirement exists because of PCI compliance, not because someone liked bcrypt. It doesn't know that the team …

The Problem


Old-school vulnerability scanners work like this:
  If response matches pattern → safe

You run a scan. It says 50 "critical" issues. You spend hours filtering. Only 8 are real. That's not security—that's a productivity killer.
Permi is an AI-powered vulnerability scanner built for today's development workflow.
Reduces false positives with intelligent filtering.
Works where you code – CLI now, VS Code & GitHub actions coming soon.
One command to scan websites or source code.
